name: In-Group Bias
description: Simply sorting people into 'us' and 'them' can skew trust, generosity, cooperation, and whose perspective gets believed. Designers run into it whenever identity cues change how fairly people are treated.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to communities, marketplaces, moderation systems, hiring/internal tools, personalization, and inclusive design: badges, labels, avatars, and segmentation can strengthen belonging for some users while excluding or penalizing others.
prevalence_note: Common in inclusive-design, trust-and-safety, marketplace, and community-design practice; not always named explicitly in basic UI curricula, but central whenever teams design for belonging, fairness, or exclusion risk.

findings.description: Across economic-game studies, people cooperate more with ingroup than outgroup members with a small-to-medium overall effect (Cohen's d = 0.32); the effect is substantially larger in interdependent situations like social dilemmas (d = 0.42) than in non-interdependent categorization-only situations like dictator games (d = 0.19), and is stronger with mutual knowledge of group membership; the pattern is better explained by ingroup favoritism than by outgroup derogation.
findings.effect_size: Cohen's d = 0.32 (overall); d = 0.19 (dictator games/no interdependence); d = 0.42 (social dilemmas/interdependence)
findings.source_title: Ingroup favoritism in cooperation: A meta-analysis

findings.description: Assigning participants to groups via a trivial, arbitrary classification (e.g., stated preference for one abstract painter over another), with no prior contact, competition, or self-interest at stake, was sufficient to produce reliable ingroup-favoring bias in the allocation of real rewards and penalties -- and participants often sacrificed maximum joint or ingroup profit in order to maximize the relative difference between ingroup and outgroup outcomes.

applications.title: In-group bias among Obama and Clinton supporters during the 2008 Democratic primary
applications.description: Researchers recruited Democrats during the 2008 presidential primary to play the Dictator Game (deciding how much of a pool of money to share with an anonymous partner), after participants indicated whether they preferred Obama or Clinton and learned their partner's preference. Run at three points -- after Clinton's concession, before the Democratic National Convention (DNC), and after the DNC -- the study found men gave significantly more money to partners who shared their candidate preference in the first two waves, an effect that disappeared after the DNC, consistent with the party's explicit effort to foster unified in-group identity there.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real political-psychology finding about intergroup favoritism during a real historical election cycle, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no UI or business decision being evaluated, only a real-world natural experiment in how political identity shapes economic generosity.
